name: Marshall Islands
summary_text: The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering consensual same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust's record of the global history of criminalisation dates the country's decriminalisation to 2005, so a visitor faces no statutory offence for consensual same-sex relations.  The most recent official country reporting in the inventory is the United States Department of State's 2015 Human Rights Report on the Marshall Islands. It recorded no reports of torture, arbitrary killings, enforced disappearances or LGBT-specific abuses, and it listed prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence among the significant problems it identified.

name: North Macedonia
summary_text: North Macedonia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1996 as a Council of Europe accession condition, and the anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity following the 2019 amendments to the Criminal Code, which explicitly list both grounds under the hate speech provisions. The Law on Primary Education adopted in July 2019 likewise introduced anti-discrimination language covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and the 2019 US Country Report found the government enforced such laws in access to government services including health care.  Legal gender recognition remains the central unresolved gap for a trans visitor carrying documents. ILGA-Europe and the ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024, working with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia, identify Legal Gender Recognition as the top priority; the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the LGR chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that requiring sex reassignment surgery before changing a gender marker violated human rights and awarded €9,000 in damages, but NGOs report the government still fails to recognise gender identity changes in identification documents. A visitor should therefore expect documents to reflect a marker that may not match presentation.  Public trans organising proceeds openly. TransFormA's March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2024 under the words "we march bravely", and the first Pride Parade took place in June 2019. A 2025 Pride Parade drew lower attendance after organisers declared it a protest, and foreign embassies pulled funding.  The protective machinery around such events is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious and continuing problem with countless reports and no meaningful state response, a reading the European Commission's country report shares. The 2019 US Country Report deemed the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases and found the LGBTQ community "still prejudiced and harassed by the society, media and the authorities", with hate speech on social media following the June 2019 Pride Parade. In September 2023 the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with sexual-orientation and gender-identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code, one documented instance of the aggravation working in practice.  Violence against LGBTI people is documented and under-reported. The 2019 US Country Report details fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student, breaking his nose; the student reported the incident to the principal but chose not to report it to police. The same report cites CSO Coalition Margini documenting 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019, including five discrimination cases and one verbal assault by a police officer, and notes most such violence goes unreported to police or institutions. It also states there are many reports about public humiliations, worker firings and even casting homosexual teenagers onto the streets due to revelation of their sexual orientations. Global Voices reported in March 2024 a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.  Same-sex relationships carry no recognition. Family law defines marriage as "a union between a man and a woman", and a 2014 government motion sought a constitutional amendment to the same effect, requiring two-thirds of MPs. A 2015 constitutional amendment that would have barred legal recognition of same-sex relations absent a two-thirds majority passed committee 72-4 and was approved in Parliament on 20 January 2015. ECRI has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.  Support infrastructure exists in the capital. The LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, offers free legal aid, and EGAL is the oldest organisation working on gay and lesbian health issues.
